claims.text: Atomic-scale lattice distortion governs yield strength in single-phase multi-component concentrated alloys.
Atomic-scale lattice distortion governs deformation and failure behavior in single-phase multi-component concentrated alloys.
Differences in constituent atomic sizes and chemical environments produce atomic-scale lattice distortions.
Lattice distortions impede dislocation motion.
Lattice distortions promote work hardening.
The promoted work hardening leads to earlier stress localization and eventual failure.
Selecting constituents with large atomic-radius differences will create greater lattice distortion than selecting constituents with similar atomic radii.
Atomic-scale lattice distortions create a heterogeneous energy landscape.
The heterogeneous energy landscape acts as a set of pinning centers that hinder dislocation glide.
Large local lattice distortions increase the activation energy for dislocation motion.
Increased dislocation pinning produces higher yield stress.
Increased dislocation pinning produces enhanced work hardening.
Under continued loading, local stress fields associated with distortion may facilitate shear banding or other failure modes.
Relative to the low-distortion baseline, the high-distortion alloy will have higher yield strength.
Relative to the low-distortion baseline, the high-distortion alloy will have a higher work-hardening rate.
Relative to the low-distortion baseline, the high-distortion alloy will show earlier or more pronounced localized deformation, such as shear-band initiation.
The high-distortion alloy will exhibit slower dislocation glide or higher residual dislocation density than the baseline.
Alloys made from constituents with similar atomic radii have minimal lattice distortion.
The proposed relationship should hold in single-phase concentrated alloys under ambient-to-moderate temperatures and controlled strain rates.
Phase separation, precipitates, or extreme temperatures may dominate the mechanical response and invalidate the proposed relationship.
